title: Lady Mary Montagu Inoculates Her Children
text:
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu knew smallpox firsthand. Her brother died of it, and in 1715 she caught it herself; she survived, but her face was scarred and she lost her eyelashes. The next year her husband was appointed British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, and she went with him to Constantinople.

There she discovered a practice unknown in England. In a letter of 1717, she described how old women, at gatherings in the autumn, scratched open a vein and placed a little matter from a smallpox sore into the wound. The children who received it fell mildly ill for a few days and were then protected for life. She wrote that she was patriotic enough to try to bring the practice into fashion in England.

In March 1718 she had her five-year-old son, Edward, inoculated in Constantinople, with the help of the embassy surgeon, Charles Maitland, and an old Greek woman. He recovered well.

Back in London, during a smallpox epidemic in 1721, she had Maitland inoculate her young daughter, this time in the presence of court physicians. The demonstration attracted attention. Experiments followed on prisoners and orphans, and in 1722 the Princess of Wales had two of her own daughters inoculated. Many doctors and clergymen attacked Lady Mary, but inoculation spread, and decades later it prepared the ground for Edward Jenner's safer vaccine.
lesson: A parent's courage to try something new for a child can benefit many other families. Watching carefully how others solve a problem can bring home a better answer.
people: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Edward Wortley Montagu, Charles Maitland
source: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Turkish Embassy Letters, letter to Sarah Chiswell (1 April 1717); Isobel Grundy, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu (1999)
